description: A team for building spherical software solutions to spherical software problems.
summary: Spherical is a free website that shows how any patch of sky changes between images taken by NASA's SPHEREx telescope, which photographs the whole sky twice a year in 102 colours of infrared light. Type an object name or coordinates and it fetches every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, straight from NASA's public archive, and plays them as a short film: blink between passes, subtract one from another, or stack hundreds of exposures along a motion to bring out faint moving objects. It adds a 2010 WISE image for a 16-year baseline, rings the stars the Gaia catalogue already knows, and draws a spectrum for anything you click. It also checks every source in the field automatically and lists what moved or changed brightness. The challenge asked for a tool that lets the public search SPHEREx images for moving objects such as nearby brown dwarfs or a distant planet; Spherical does that for any position, with no account, download or API key. It matters because SPHEREx records hundreds of millions of objects, far more than scientists can inspect, and moving or changing objects are found by comparing images. In test scans of about 1,000 fields the tool measured the motion of Barnard's Star to within 4% of the catalogue value and turned up 14 stars whose brightness changes are not in the variable-star catalogues we checked.
details:
What it does

Spherical turns SPHEREx's archive into something anyone can look through. Enter a name ("Barnard's Star"), coordinates, or press "Take me somewhere random". The site then:

  • finds every SPHEREx exposure covering that position (typically 300 to 500) and fetches a small cutout of each;
  • Blink: shows one combined image per six-monthly SPHEREx pass, plus a 2010 WISE image, so anything that moved jumps;
  • Difference: subtracts one pass from another, so a mover appears as a blue and orange pair and a star that brightened stands out;
  • Shift and stack: slides every exposure along a trial motion and adds them, which brings out movers too faint for a single image;
  • Exposures: shows each single image with its wavelength and NASA's per-pixel quality flags;
  • lets you choose any of the telescope's six infrared bands;
  • rings known stars from ESA's Gaia catalogue at the place they were on the date shown, so a moving dot without a ring stands out;
  • draws a spectrum (up to 102 wavelengths, downloadable as CSV) for any dot you click;
  • Whole field: checks every source automatically for motion since 2010 and for brightness changes between passes, and lists the ones worth a look;
  • puts the whole view into the page address, so any finding can be shared or embedded.

The start page explains the mission to a general reader, with a live 3D diagram of how SPHEREx scans the sky, and a 30-second guided tour introduces the controls.

How it works

The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Small Cloudflare Functions ask NASA's IRSA archive which SPHEREx images cover a position, then read only the few kilobytes needed from each 60 MB image file in NASA's public SPHEREx bucket on AWS, using HTTP range requests. They decode the FITS headers, the distortion-corrected sky coordinates, the Rice-compressed quality flags and the wavelength map, and return a small tile, cached in Cloudflare R2. In the browser, WebGPU aligns, stacks and subtracts hundreds of tiles in real time (with a canvas fallback where WebGPU is missing). The same pipeline reads the 2010 AllWISE atlas for the long baseline. Nothing is pre-computed and no data is copied into the project, so new SPHEREx releases appear by adding one line of configuration.

The page also offers its functions to AI agents through the browser's WebMCP interface (look_at_sky, list_changes, inspect_position, set_view, get_view), so software can search the sky with the same tool people use.

What it has found

To test it, an AI agent ran the tool over about 1,000 fields, first through the WebMCP tools and then with a script that runs the same code.

  • Barnard's Star, found without being told where to look: 9.97 arcseconds per year (Gaia: 10.39). Teegarden's Star and Epsilon Indi were recovered to within 1%.
  • In 608 fields away from the Milky Way, 19 fast-moving stars were picked out, with speeds that match the CatWISE and Gaia catalogues. All 19 were already known. No new moving object was found.
  • 14 stars show brightness changes that are not recorded in SIMBAD, the AAVSO Variable Star Index (VizieR copy), Gaia DR3 or the ZTF and WISE variable-star catalogues. Each is confirmed as variable by ten years of independent NEOWISE measurements. They are listed in the repository with draft reports for the AAVSO.

Limits, stated plainly: the 14 candidates have not been confirmed by anyone else; stars like these are common in the Milky Way, so they are new to the catalogues rather than rare; SPHEREx's 6 arcsecond pixels make faint sources hard to place, which caused false alarms the scan now rejects; and the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE 0855, is too faint for SPHEREx single exposures.

Why it matters

Most nearby brown dwarfs found in recent years were spotted by volunteers comparing WISE images by eye. SPHEREx adds a new all-sky map every six months with a spectrum at every point, and each new pass makes motion easier to see. Spherical gives the public, students and researchers a direct way to look, and gives software agents the same access.

Tools and languages

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebGPU (WGSL shaders), Cloudflare Pages, Functions and R2, Node.js for the offline scan scripts. No frameworks or build step.
